title: Bad comfort (Job 4–5)
hookLine: his friends insist he must have sinned; they're wrong
tomorrow: I know that my redeemer lives

cards: Everything happens for a reason. God doesn't give you more than you can handle. Maybe this is a wake-up call.

At least you're young. Most of us have heard sentences like these at the worst moment of our lives, or, if we're honest, said them. They're usually meant kindly, by people who love us and can't stand the silence.

And they can land like a slap. The book of Job has a name for the people who say them, coined by Job himself. But first, the man who speaks right after Job's curse: Eliphaz, the gentlest of the three.

teach.b: Eliphaz begins politely, almost apologetically: if we try to talk with you, will you be upset? He reminds Job that Job has comforted others in his time. Fair enough.
Then the turn, in the King James Bible: "Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?" Innocent people don't get destroyed.
"Even as I have seen, they that plow iniquity, and sow wickedness, reap the same." You reap what you sow; do the math.
He even describes a frightening night vision to back himself up: "Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up."
And he has lines that sound like they belong on a wall: "Yet man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward." Here's the strange part.
A lot of what Eliphaz says is true somewhere. The apostle Paul even quotes him, in First Corinthians, as scripture. The problem isn't the sayings.
It's where he points them: a general rule fitted onto a grieving man the reader knows is blameless. He explains Job's pain to Job.

Job's reply comes a few chapters later: "miserable comforters are ye all." Centuries later, in John's Gospel, the disciples see a man born blind and ask Jesus: who sinned, this man, or his parents? Jesus answers: neither.
And at the very end of Job, God himself will say these friends got it wrong.

teach.h: THEY CAME TO COMFORT, THEN EXPLAINED.
teach.b: They came to comfort. They sat in silence beautifully. Then they started explaining.

how: Christian pastors and chaplains often study Job's friends as a warning in pastoral care training: listen first, and do not tell sufferers their pain is a punishment.

o: a friend who stays far away while you are grieving
kind words that arrive far too late to help anyone
true-sounding sayings used to explain someone's suffering

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: who sinned, this man or his parents?

s: many of his sayings are true in general; Paul even quotes one. the problem is aiming them at Job.
Eliphaz tells Job that innocent people don't perish
"who ever perished, being innocent?" the reader already knows Job is blameless.
at the end of the book, God sides with the friends
God says the friends have not spoken rightly; that comes in chapter 42.

games.q: you're Eliphaz. your friend has lost everything and just cursed the day he was born. you finally speak. what do you say?
o: remind him that innocent people don't suffer like this.
tell him he's right to grieve, and stay.
describe a frightening dream that proves your point.
games.why: Eliphaz chooses the first, and the vision. the book shows that it fails: Job calls them "miserable comforters", and God later says they were wrong.

practice: Think back over the last few weeks to a moment someone told you something hard and you reached for a reason: maybe it's for the best, or at least.

Find it gently, without beating yourself up, and replay it, this time saying: that sounds really hard, I'm here. If you pray, ask for the grace to sit before you speak; if not, just rehearse the quieter answer.

wordCard.voice: Bad comfort. Job's friends, meaning well, turn true-sounding sayings on a suffering man and tell him he must have deserved it.

orig.note: Hebrew: comforters of trouble, comforters who make it worse. Job's name for his friends in 16:2.

carryVoice: Your line: don't explain their pain. Eliphaz's sayings were true somewhere, just not there. Day four hundred forty-five, done.
